idiom_name: top-level private (file) and internal (module) with a narrow internal object as the attorney; private constructors where construction itself is the grant
implementation_notes: Kotlin replaces C++ friendship with two scopes: a top-level declaration marked private is visible in its file only, internal is visible everywhere in the same module (a Gradle source set, Maven project or IDEA module), and a class member marked private is visible inside that class including all its members, so a nested class or a member function can act as the gate (kotlinlang.org, visibility modifiers). The idiomatic realization is to keep the implementation internal or file-private and expose a deliberately narrow function or object as the attorney; a private primary constructor (class C private constructor(...)) is the language's own way to make construction itself the grant. The hand-built attorney is still justified when a single collaborator in another module must be the only caller - Kotlin cannot express that - and the module boundary is then only as narrow as the module.
pitfalls: internal is module-wide: every file compiled together sees the declaration, and the test source set is allowed to reach main's internal declarations, so the boundary is far wider than 'one helper'.

Top-level private is file-scoped: moving the implementation or the helper into another file silently changes the grant (usually into a compile error, but the split is easy to overlook in review), so internal is the stabler choice for a cross-file attorney.

A member's private visibility covers the class and its members only - an extension function declared elsewhere, even in the same file, gets no access - so a helper written as an extension cannot be the attorney; nest it, make it a member, or widen to internal.
